title: Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone
gist: Rocket Report 9.20 contrasts SpaceX's first-ever midair catch of a Starship upper stage with ULA's first total Vulcan failure, which destroyed 40 Amazon Leo satellites and threatens ~70 booked Amazon and Space Force launches (preliminary cause: inadequate fuel supply to BE-4 engines, not the engines). Also: ICEYE's $2.2B+ bid for Avio, NATO's Starlift launch brokerage, Stoke completing its Zenith engine, LandSpace engine refurbishment, Relativity's Terran R progress, and Google booking New Glenn for orbital AI compute.

insights.claim: On November 14 SpaceX made the first successful tower catch of a Starship upper stage after nearly a day in orbit, though the Super Heavy booster was lost at sea; rapid reuse of both stages underpins SpaceX's commercial ambitions and US strategic space goals.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Moves SpaceX materially closer to full reusability and step-change launch cost reduction, widening its moat.
insights.quote: It’s hard to overstate the significance of the moment.

insights.claim: ULA suffered its first-ever total launch failure when a Vulcan rocket carrying 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff; it was the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon booked to build its Starlink competitor.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Delays Amazon Leo deployment and strengthens Starlink's lead in satellite broadband.
insights.locator: Vulcan fails to deliver for Amazon.

insights.claim: Vulcan is contracted for roughly half of US Space Force national security launches over the next few years, and Space Force and Amazon together have booked some 70 Vulcan launches, so the failure ripples across the US space industry.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Grounding Vulcan shifts national-security and constellation launch demand toward SpaceX Falcon 9.
insights.locator: Last weekend was a picture of the US launch business

insights.claim: ULA's preliminary review attributes the Vulcan failure to inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines rather than engine performance, which is good news for Blue Origin, whose New Glenn uses a similar design; Vulcan's solid boosters performed as expected after nozzle failures on two prior flights.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Limits contagion to Blue Origin's New Glenn program; ULA-specific fix may be faster.
insights.quote: not from the performance of the engines

insights.claim: Finnish radar-satellite company ICEYE, valued at over $12 billion, is seeking to buy Italian rocket maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion to create Europe's first vertically integrated end-to-end space company.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Space-sector M&A premium for launch assets; Avio shareholders may benefit and European vertical integration accelerates.
insights.locator: Europe’s leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker.

insights.claim: ICEYE's push to acquire Avio is driven by European demand for sovereign space and defense capability and its need for rides to orbit as SpaceX's Falcon 9, which launched most ICEYE satellites, nears retirement; Avio's Vega C has a government backlog but little commercial success.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Falcon 9 retirement creates launch-access anxiety for SpaceX-dependent satellite operators.

insights.claim: ICEYE sells radar surveillance data to governments including Ukraine, which uses its imagery to target and track Russian troop movements.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Commercial SAR imagery is battle-proven defense revenue — supports defense-space valuations.

insights.claim: NATO launched Starlift, letting 11 countries pool military launch needs and buy commercial launch slots including short-notice crisis launches, plus a Global Data Marketplace; NATO's tech agency will offer about $2.7 billion in contracts over two years spanning space, AI, cyber and command-and-control.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: New multinational demand pool for commercial launch and space data providers.

insights.claim: Stoke Space finished development of its methane Zenith engine and is shipping flight engines weekly to Cape Canaveral; seven Zeniths give Nova's reusable first stage about 700,000 lbf, with a 24-thruster, regeneratively cooled heat-shield second stage aimed at full reuse and first launch expected next year.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Stoke is a credible fully-reusable medium-lift entrant to watch in 2027.
insights.locator: Stoke wraps up booster engine development.

insights.claim: Relativity Space's partially reusable Terran R could launch next year absent major setbacks, having completed its first-stage thrust structure with 13 Aeon engines and a second-stage all-up test firing at Stennis, while building its Cape Canaveral pad.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Adds medium-lift capacity competition in 2027 as heavy-lift slots tighten.
insights.locator: Relativity makes progress with Terran R.

insights.claim: China's LandSpace says it refurbished and re-tested all nine methane engines recovered from its Zhuque-3 booster's August orbital landing, though the booster itself toppled after touchdown; Zhuque-3 is one of two Chinese rockets to land a booster after orbital launch.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: China's commercial launch sector is closing the reusability gap with US players.
insights.locator: China’s LandSpace reports rocket reuse milestone.

insights.claim: Google booked a 2029 New Glenn 7x2 launch for Project Suncatcher orbital AI data-center satellites as US commercial heavy-lift capacity fills through 2030, raising the question of whether orbital compute ambitions are tenable without owning a launch vehicle.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Heavy-lift scarcity confers leverage on launch owners over hyperscaler space-compute plans.
insights.locator: Google taps Blue Origin for AI launch.

insights.claim: Russia's Vostochny Cosmodrome, which by some measures cost over $5 billion, averages about two launches a year; its single 2026 Soyuz-2.1b launch carried dual-use imaging satellites and CubeSats for arms maker NPO Kaisant to support secure communications for Russian drones over Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Russia is militarizing small-sat constellations for drone warfare despite underused launch infrastructure.
insights.locator: Soyuz flies from Russia’s Far East.
